stage_description: The geriatric stage begins at around six years — a threshold not every guinea pig reaches, since the average lifespan is five to seven years. The animal weakens noticeably: muscle mass declines, sight and hearing fade, and several chronic conditions may exist at once. The pet sleeps a great deal and moves cautiously. Care focuses on keeping it comfortable, easing chronic conditions, and preserving a good quality of life.
nutrition: Feeding is adapted to what an old guinea pig can manage, while keeping hay unlimited and daily vitamin C non-negotiable. If teeth or weakness make chewing hard, pellets and vegetables can be moistened or chopped, and if the pet stops eating, a vet may prescribe a special recovery formula for syringe feeding. Preventing dehydration and weight loss is key — weigh the pet often and offer the most appetising, easy-to-eat foods.
activity: Exertion is kept to calm, undemanding movement. Set up single-level housing with soft bedding, a warm and draught-free spot, and a short path to food, water, and a hide. Check the skin of a less mobile animal regularly for pressure sores and keep the coat clean. Gentle handling and the presence of a compatible companion help keep it calm; avoid abrupt changes and stress.
veterinary_check_frequency: Veterinary oversight increases — exams every three to six months, or more often where chronic disease needs monitoring. The vet checks weight, teeth, joints, and heart and kidney function and helps fine-tune supportive care and quality of life. At home, keep a log of weight, appetite, drinking, and activity, and report any change to the vet.
dental_care: Dental problems are especially common in old age and may call for regular veterinary trimming of overgrown cheek teeth. Keep offering hay to chew, and where that is hard, softened food that still contains fibre. Drooling, dropping food, weight loss, and bad breath are signals to have the teeth examined without delay.
warning_signs: At this age any new symptom deserves attention: refusing food or water, no droppings, sudden weakness, laboured or rapid breathing, an inability to move, signs of pain (a hunched posture, teeth grinding), or seizures. In a guinea pig, going off food is always an emergency. It is also wise to discuss quality-of-life questions with the vet in advance.
